title: Postgres semantics is an assumption
objective: Complete the assumptions field of the claim you minted in S6.L8 from three histories, name each assumed clause, and turn each clause that can be turned into a configured or an enforced one.

segments.title: What your checker did not see

blocks.md: In S6.L8 you minted a claim from what your checker saw. This lesson is about what it did not see.

choice.prompt: Your checker accepted all n recorded SERIALIZABLE histories. What does that establish about production?

options.text: Only that these n histories were serializable.
options.why: It is a `TESTED [T]` result over the histories it saw. Production rests on clauses no history covers.
That generalizes from tests to every transaction.

options.text: That PostgreSQL has no isolation bugs.
options.why: A release of PostgreSQL once had one, as the dated incident below shows.

options.text: That PostgreSQL behaves as its manual documents.
options.why: A serializable history is consistent with the manual, and shows nothing about other histories.

blocks.md: Three histories show where the claim is thin. First, read skew.

blocks.direction: Replay shows: txn A reads account 1, txn B's transfer commits, and txn A reads account 2. Add up what txn A saw.
blocks.after: Txn A saw 100 and then 150, a total of 250 250, though every committed state totals 200. Your checker rejects that report. READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot for each statement, so a reader that spans two statements can see two committed states.

blocks.md: Mixed levels. Txn A runs SERIALIZABLE and txn B runs READ COMMITTED.
blocks.direction: Replay shows: both sessions read the team total before either debits, then each debits and commits.

options.text: Yes: txn B fails with a serialization failure.
options.why: Only SERIALIZABLE transactions are tracked for read-write cycles, and txn B is not one.

options.text: Yes: txn A fails with a serialization failure.
options.why: The guarantee covers a set of SERIALIZABLE transactions, and this set has one member.

options.text: No: both commit, and the team total goes below zero.
options.why: The manual's guarantee covers "any set of successfully committed concurrent Serializable transactions" (§13.2.3, read 2026-10-23). Txn B is outside that set.

blocks.after: Both committed; the team sank to -100 -100. One writer at a weaker level removes the protection from every cycle it joins.

blocks.md: Third, a toy history shaped like the cycle Jepsen reported (see the dated incident below).
A toy G2-item history at SERIALIZABLE.
blocks.direction: Check asserts: some serial order gives each transaction the reads it reported.

code.text:
-- items x and y both start at 0
txn A   read x -> 0;   write y = 1;   committed
txn B   read y -> 0;   write x = 1;   committed

search  serial orders of the 2 committed transactions
bound   at most 8 transactions

blocks.after: The checker rejects it {{run:RUN-history-g2item}}. With txn A first, txn B would have read y = 1. With txn B first, txn A would have read x = 1. A SERIALIZABLE database must never commit this pair.

blocks.md:
Your claim rests on three clauses. Give each the strongest stamp it can carry.

1. **Every writer is SERIALIZABLE.** The guarantee has a condition: "If the Serializable transaction isolation level is used for all writes and for all reads which need a consistent view of the data" (§13.4.1, read 2026-10-23). Set `default_transaction_isolation = serializable` and read it back from each session: CONFIGURED [C]. Add a check in each transaction, as the manual suggests with "checks of the transaction isolation level in triggers": ENFORCED [E].
2. **PostgreSQL behaves as documented.** ASSUMED [A]. You can narrow it: the regression spec for the bug Jepsen found, `update-conflict-out.spec`, passes on the version you pin {{run:RUN-pg-catalog}} (row H21), and the course re-runs it on a schedule. One history is evidence, not a stamp.
3. **Nothing reads a replica.** ASSUMED [A]. The protection "does not yet extend to hot standby mode … or logical replicas" (§13.4.1), and SERIALIZABLE "is not yet available in hot standby" (§26.4.5). A report served from a standby is outside your claim. The course plants this clause as a seam here, and S7.L8 is where it cracks.

If you built kernelspace's pool conformance, re-stamp it the same way: a lockstep run over one deterministic traffic script is TESTED [T] · n ticks · 1 script.

choice.prompt: A claim's strip has three segments: the proposition of the model, the correspondence, and the requirement fit. Every session of your pool reads back `default_transaction_isolation = serializable`. Where does that evidence go, and with which stamp?

options.text: Proposition of the model: `TESTED [T] · n histories`
options.why: That is what the checker's runs earn. A setting says nothing about histories.

options.text: Correspondence: `CONFIGURED [C] · read back from each session`
options.why: It says how the running system relates to the model, and a setting read back from the system is CONFIGURED [C], with its source.

options.text: Requirement fit: `ASSUMED [A] · fit for purpose is a judgment`
options.why: Requirement fit does stay assumed, but a setting read back is evidence about the running system: the correspondence.
A setting alone blocks nothing: a client can still start a transaction at a weaker level.

options.text: A claim that assumes no replica reads still covers a report served from a standby.
options.why: A standby is exactly what the clause excludes.

options.text: Reading `serializable` back from every session shows every transaction ran SERIALIZABLE.
options.why: That is CONFIGURED [C]. A client can start a transaction at a weaker level.

options.text: With one writer at READ COMMITTED, the SERIALIZABLE guarantee does not cover that writer's transactions.
options.why: The guarantee covers a set of SERIALIZABLE transactions, as the mixed-levels cell showed.

options.text: Jepsen's 2020 finding means the SERIALIZABLE of the version you pin cannot be trusted at all.
options.why: The bug was fixed, and its regression spec passes on your version.

blocks.title: PostgreSQL 12.3, June 2020
blocks.md: Jepsen found that PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE "exhibited G2-item under normal operation", confirmed in 9.5.22, 10.13, 11.8, 12.3 and 13 (https://jepsen.io/analyses/postgresql-12.3, 2020-06-12, §3.2, read 2026-10-23).

blocks.title: Production twin: Jepsen
blocks.md: Jepsen's analysis and PostgreSQL's `update-conflict-out.spec` (pin {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}). What did the regression test pin, and which line of your claim depends on it?

blocks.title: Reading
blocks.md: Roadmap reading for Stage 6: PostgreSQL's chapter on transaction isolation. Here, read §13.4.1 (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/applevel-consistency.html, read 2026-10-23) and the caveats in §26.4.5 (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/hot-standby.html, read 2026-10-23).

RUN-history-g2item.title: Souffle 2.5 reads three transaction histories as dependency graphs: the toy G2-item history of Jepsen's PostgreSQL 12.3 report (h1) and AUD-6.3's two recorded PostgreSQL 18.6 histories, read committed (h2) and serializable (h3); it finds a cycle of anti-dependencies in h1 and h2 and none in h3
verdict_lines: [h1] G2-item: a cycle of dependencies with an anti-dependency edge
[h2] G2-item: a cycle of dependencies with an anti-dependency edge
notes: The facts are written by hand, one file per history (inputs/hN/), each line traced in a comment of history.md to the run log it comes from: h1 to the shape of the G2-item anomaly Jepsen reported (https://jepsen.io/analyses/postgresql-12.3), not to Jepsen's own history files; h2 and h3 to RUN-pg-pool-levels q2-p1 and q1-p1.

g2.dl derives write-read, write-write and read-write (anti-dependency) edges between committed transactions from the reads and the version order of the writes (Adya's direct serialization graph), and reports a cycle that contains a read-write edge as g2item. run.sh runs souffle once per history and prefixes each output line with "[hN] ".

RUN-pg-catalog.title: PostgreSQL 18.6 isolation catalog: rows H01-H24 in isolationtester format, the upstream baseline, the SERIALIZABLE behavior of 40001, 40P01, 23505 and 23P01, and the seeded GEN-anomaly-id grid

budget.data_directory: tmpfs, 2g (a speed choice; visibility rules do not depend on it)
budget.network: default bridge, unused during the runs
budget.step_timeout: PG_TEST_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT=10 (the tester cancels a step after 20 s and exits after 40 s); 2 for the one-permutation fallback
budget.cpu: no cap; other tasks used the host at the same time, so durations are noisy

verdict_lines: RESULT rows-recorded: PASS (24 of 24 catalog rows recorded; 24 specs run, 366 permutations, each output beside its spec)
RESULT upstream-baseline: PASS (25 of 25 upstream specs print exactly the expected output of the 18.6 source tree)
RESULT stable-across-passes: PASS (50 of 50 row, upstream and variant outputs byte-identical in two passes)
RESULT sqlstate-join: PASS (564 errors printed by the tester in the row runs, 564 logged by the server, matched error for error and session by session; each message maps to one SQLSTATE)
RESULT upstream-variant receipt-report-s3-read-write: INFO (session s3 declared READ WRITE instead of READ ONLY; 210 permutations, 48 end with an error)
RESULT grid-model-check: PASS (3717 histories; 1337 lock waits observed, all predicted by the lock model; 0 cells needed the one-permutation fallback)
RESULT grid-stable-across-passes: PASS (3717 histories compared across two passes; 0 differ)
RESULT grid-t1: PASS (read-modify-write: 558 recorded histories against a target of 200; display half 279, graded half 279; patterns {'rmw2': 378, 'cond2': 108, 'rmw3': 72})
RESULT grid-t2: PASS (write skew: 1080 recorded histories against a target of 200; display half 540, graded half 540; patterns {'teamsum2': 540, 'holds2': 540})
RESULT grid-t3: PASS (read skew: 1134 recorded histories against a target of 200; display half 569, graded half 565; patterns {'readskew2': 270, 'readskew3': 324, 'readskew2-mixed': 540})

RESULT grid-t4: PASS (serialization failure or deadlock: 837 recorded histories against a target of 200; display half 413, graded half 424; patterns {'opposite2': 288, 'ordered2': 90, 'retry-overflow': 27, 'retry-unique': 18, 'retry-holds': 162, 'retry-cond': 36, 'retry-opposite': 216})
RESULT grid-excluded: INFO (after abort 108; unstable 0; dropped 0)
ROW H01 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: both commit, final 20, the second debit's write returns 20 -> 20. SERIALIZABLE, only expected before, is recorded: 40001.
ROW H02 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the waiting statement updates 0 rows. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, only expected before, are recorded: 40001.
ROW H03 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the DELETE removes 0 rows and a hits = 10 row exists before and after. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H04 [agrees]: The reader's two reads total 250 at READ COMMITTED and 200 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.
ROW H05 [agrees]: Both commit at READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ with a team total of -100; at SERIALIZABLE the second committer fails with 40001 and the total is 50.
ROW H06 [agrees]: Both commit at READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ (160 held against 100); at SERIALIZABLE one fails with 40001 and 80 stays held.
ROW H07 [agrees]: Run from the upstream specs: REPEATABLE READ gives s3 a state no serial order shows; SERIALIZABLE aborts s2 with 40001 (-2); DEFERRABLE makes s3 wait (-3).
ROW H08 [agrees]: 6 of 210 permutations fail with s3 READ ONLY; the READ WRITE variant is measured here, not read from the spec comment.
ROW H09 [agrees]: The second count is 3 at READ COMMITTED, 2 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.
ROW H10 [agrees]: With one session SERIALIZABLE and the other READ COMMITTED both commit, in both assignments and both commit orders; with both SERIALIZABLE one fails with 40001.
ROW H11 [agrees]: A sequential scan aborts a SERIALIZABLE transaction that shares no row with the other; the same transactions on an index scan over distant keys both commit.

ROW H12 [agrees, with additions]: 23505 and 23P01 appear under SERIALIZABLE; which of 40001 and 23505 appears depends on whether the failing session checked first and on the order, and a whole-command retry with a re-check ends without error where a blind retry fails again.
ROW H13 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the statement waits, then updates the row it could not see. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H14 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: 23505, no restart. REPEATABLE READ: 23505. SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H15 [agrees]: Disjoint claims at all three levels; the count through SKIP LOCKED is 0 while 4 jobs are pending.
ROW H16 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED returns the rows out of order; REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE raise 40001; FOR UPDATE in a subquery returns them in order.
ROW H17 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: mallory sees 'secret from mallory'. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: her locking read fails with 40001, so it is prevented by failure.
ROW H18 [agrees]: CHECK accepts NULL, the guarded UPDATE skips the NULL row, USING hides it, WITH CHECK raises 42501; the same at all three levels.
ROW H19 [agrees]: 22003 'bigint out of range' at all three levels; the balance is unchanged; sum(bigint) is numeric.
ROW H20 [agrees]: Row 1 is never delivered: the mark is 2, both ids exist, the next poll returns nothing; the same at all three levels.
ROW H21 [agrees]: Both permutations of the regression test end with bar's 40001, the output the upstream file expects.

ROW H22 [differs]: Ascending order removes the deadlock and both commit at READ COMMITTED. At REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, 4 of the 6 ascending-order permutations still fail with 40001 (first updater wins), so ordering is no substitute for the retry.
ROW H23 [agrees]: B's COMMIT fails with 40001; its retry reads 20 available, the guard refuses (0 rows) and nothing is written.
ROW H24 [agrees]: REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: B fails with 40001 and its retry updates 0 rows. READ COMMITTED: no error, 0 rows.
notes: The tester is PostgreSQL's own isolationtester, built from the 18.6 source tarball and run against the Debian-packaged 18.6 server of the postgres:18 image; it is not statespace isorun (W4-T16).

isolationtester prints errors as 'ERROR:  <message>' without a SQLSTATE. SQLSTATEs come from the server's csv log: each session's application_name is '<tag>/<session>', and for every session the messages the tester printed must equal the messages the server logged, in order; a mismatch stops the run.
NULL prints as an empty cell in isolationtester output; an empty string prints the same way.

A session that continues after an error meets 'current transaction is aborted' (25P02) at its next write. Those follow-on errors stay in the row outputs, as after_abort in the index, and keep a history out of the GEN-anomaly-id pool.
The lock model that decides which interleavings cannot hang the tester is sound and incomplete; every lock wait the tester reported was one the model predicted.
The grid's 'half' split, the target counts and the retry patterns are design defaults [D], not measurements.
Nothing was emulated: no browser, phone, hosted service or other PostgreSQL version was involved. PGlite is a different instrument (W0-S08).

notes: Recorded by W1 follow-up 1 (task_label W1-followup-1); the task field is left out because run@1 accepts only W<n>-S<nn> or W<n>-T<nn> there.

The cell is in isolationtester format; isolationtester itself was not run (it is built from the PostgreSQL source tree, as W0-S09 did for RUN-pg-catalog). iso_driver.py, written by the recorder, replays it with psycopg 3.3.6 on Python 3.13.12 in the bench image: one connection per session in autocommit mode (BEGIN and COMMIT are steps), each step sent with the simple query protocol so a step of two statements returns both results, a step reported as waiting once pg_isolation_test_session_is_blocked says so (the function isolationtester uses), a permutation not run when it needs a step from a session that is still waiting, a fresh setup before each permutation, and the check query on a separate connection after both sessions finish. The server ran in postgres:18@sha256:74935e72241653ca55e0414067e6d8763aceb8a810eb51b452253ec3dcfc4336 on its own user network with --memory=6g; before the driver started, the recorder waited until docker logs showed "database system is ready to accept connections" twice and pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 exited 0 (at most 120 polls, 0.5 s apart). argv lists the commands in order; started_at, duration_s and exit_code are those of the driver's run.

The cell's debit steps carry no guard (its comments say "only if a_total allowed it"; both totals read 200, so the guard H10 writes in SQL would have allowed both debits); they ran as the cell writes them. values.mixed holds each session's COMMIT outcome and the state after; values.control_both_serializable the same for the control.

notes: Recorded by W1 follow-up 1 (task_label W1-followup-1); the task field is left out because run@1 accepts only W<n>-S<nn> or W<n>-T<nn> there.
A pin is the commit a ref pointed to when ls-remote read it; read_at is that instant. The record is stale 60 days after its started_at and is refreshed by re-running the commands in argv.

git ls-remote was first run with several ref patterns per command (HEAD plus refs/tags/... or refs/heads/...); for leanprover/lean4 and postgres/postgres that printed nothing with exit 0. The recorded run uses one pattern per command; the pin for lean4 tags and PR 14577 uses a trailing * pattern, and every matching ref is kept in refs.

refs/pull/14577/merge is not advertised; only refs/pull/14577/head is. The v4.35.0 tag points at eb6cafb7290e8bd5f2937522d8d804f58f02bafc, the commit the bench image's Lean prints in its version string.

Twin cards that name no git repository are not pinned here: Stripe's "Idempotent requests" API page, the Zanzibar paper (USENIX ATC 2019), Jepsen's PostgreSQL 12.3 analysis, the arXiv papers on Cedar and CCF, SymCert (FMCAD 2026) and the AWS Automated Reasoning checks pages. Each card states its own read date.
Isabelle is developed in Mercurial; the pin is from its GitHub mirror, isabelle-prover/mirror-isabelle.
input sha256 for each command is the SHA-256 of the lines it printed, joined by newlines with a trailing newline.
